outline.title: The Problem with Direct DOM Updates
Refs: Escaping to the Real DOM

blocks.text: What is the DOM?

React never asks you to touch the browser DOM directly — yet everything it renders ends up there. This module explains what the DOM is, why React puts a virtual copy in front of it, and how updates actually reach the screen.

The Document Object Model is the browser's live, in-memory tree built from your HTML. Every tag becomes a node that JavaScript can read and modify — and every modification can make the browser recalculate what the page looks like.

blocks.caption: The browser parses HTML into a tree of nodes. Your entire React app mounts inside a single one of them — usually <div id="root">.

blocks.text: The Problem with Direct DOM Updates
Changing the DOM is easy — paying for it is not. Each change can send the browser through its whole rendering pipeline before pixels reach the screen.

blocks.caption: One DOM write can trigger style recalculation, layout, paint, and compositing. Do it hundreds of times per interaction and the page starts to stutter.

blocks.title: Typical cost of one update (ms)
blocks.sideText: Reads are cheap, writes are pricier, and anything that forces synchronous layout or repaint dominates the frame budget — a 60fps frame gives you only about 16ms total.

blocks.text: Reading layout (offsetHeight) right after writing styles in a loop forces the browser to reflow again and again — the classic 'layout thrashing' bug.
Virtual DOM Explained

React's answer is to never let you talk to the real DOM during rendering. Components return a description of the UI — a tree of plain JavaScript objects. Creating and comparing these objects is orders of magnitude cheaper than touching real nodes.

nodes.label: Real DOM
nodes.sublabel: The browser's actual tree. Slow to mutate, expensive to layout and paint.

nodes.label: Virtual DOM
nodes.sublabel: Plain JS objects describing the UI. Cheap to create, cheap to compare.

nodes.label: Shadow DOM
nodes.sublabel: Browser encapsulation for web components — unrelated to React's virtual DOM.

blocks.alt: Old virtual tree compared with new virtual tree, only the changed node is patched
blocks.caption: React keeps the previous virtual tree, builds a new one on every render, and patches only the nodes that differ.
setState never touches the DOM directly. React re-renders to a new virtual tree, diffs it against the old one, and applies the minimal set of real DOM operations.

blocks.text: Reconciliation & Diffing
Reconciliation is the algorithm that decides what changed. A perfect tree diff would cost O(n³), so React uses heuristics that finish in O(n) and are right nearly all of the time.

blocks.caption: Every update runs the same loop: state changes, components render a new virtual tree, React diffs it, and the commit phase writes the result to the real DOM.

items: Different element type → React throws the whole subtree away and rebuilds it
Same type → React keeps the node and updates only the changed props
Same component type → state is preserved and the render is reused
Lists → children are matched by key, not by their position

blocks.title: Update time as the app grows (ms)
blocks.sideText: With a handful of nodes, direct DOM code can even be faster. As the app grows, diffing wins: update cost tracks what changed, not how big the page is.

blocks.text: Keys in Lists
When React diffs a list, it needs to know which item is which across renders. Keys give list items a stable identity — without them, React falls back to matching by position.

blocks.sideText: A stable key (like a database id) lets the diff algorithm move, insert, and delete list items precisely — keeping each row's DOM and state attached to the right item.

blocks.text: Avoid array indexes as keys on lists that can reorder, insert, or delete. Rows keep the wrong state — a checkbox checked on row 2 stays on 'position 2' even after the items shift.
Refs: Escaping to the Real DOM
Sometimes you genuinely need the real node — focusing an input, measuring size, scrolling, or driving a non-React library. Refs are React's official escape hatch.

blocks.sideText: useRef gives you a stable container object. React fills .current with the real DOM node after commit — so effects are the safe place to use it.

blocks.caption: The ref is empty during render and only points at the DOM node once React has committed.

blocks.text: Batching & Concurrent Updates
React does not flush every setState to the DOM immediately. Updates are batched into a single render pass, and since React 18 the renderer can even pause and resume work to keep the page responsive.
Since React 18, multiple setState calls in the same handler are batched into one re-render — even inside promises, timeouts, and native event callbacks.

blocks.title: Where a typical update spends time
blocks.sideText: Inside a typical update, React's own diffing is only part of the story — the browser still spends real time painting whatever actually changed.

blocks.text: Common Pitfalls

items: Mutating the DOM behind React's back — your changes get overwritten on the next render
Reading layout during render — forces a sync reflow; do it in useEffect or useLayoutEffect
Index keys on reorderable lists — state sticks to the wrong rows
Overusing refs for data that should live in state — the UI stops reacting to it

blocks.text: Key Takeaways

items: The DOM is the browser's live tree; React renders to it through a cheap virtual copy
Diffing makes update cost proportional to what changed, not to app size
Keys give list items identity across renders — never index on dynamic lists
Refs are the official escape hatch to real nodes; read them after commit
Batching means the DOM updates once per event, not once per setState

blocks.text: Quick Quiz
Check yourself before moving on:

questions.question: Why does React rebuild an entire subtree when the element type changes?
options: It's a bug the team hasn't fixed yet
Different element types are assumed to produce incompatible trees, so React doesn't try to diff their contents
It only happens when keys are missing
React always rebuilds every subtree on every render
questions.explanation: This is one of React's core diffing heuristics: a type change (e.g. <div> to <span>) is treated as a completely different tree, so React unmounts the old one and mounts the new one instead of trying to patch it.

questions.question: What goes wrong when you use array indexes as keys on a sortable or filterable list?
options: The app throws a runtime error
Nothing — indexes are the recommended key for all lists
Row state (like a checked checkbox) can stick to the wrong item after the list reorders
The list renders in reverse order
questions.explanation: React matches list children by key. If the key is just the index, inserting or reordering items shifts which index maps to which item — so state that was attached to 'position 2' stays there even though a different item now sits at position 2.

questions.question: Why is useEffect (or useLayoutEffect) the safe place to read ref.current?
options: During render, React hasn't committed the DOM yet, so ref.current is still null
useEffect runs before the component renders
It isn't — refs can be read anywhere safely
questions.explanation: React fills in ref.current only after it commits changes to the real DOM. Effects run after commit, which is why reading a ref during render returns null or a stale node.
